{{About|a theorem in complex analysis||Hurwitz's theorem (disambiguation){{!}}Hurwitz's theorem}}
{{Short description|Limit of roots of sequence of functions}}
In [[mathematics]] and in particular the field of [[complex analysis]],  '''Hurwitz's theorem''' is a theorem associating the [[Zero (complex analysis)|zeroes]] of a [[sequence]] of [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]], [[Compact convergence|compact]] [[Uniform convergence#Definition|locally uniformly convergent]] functions with that of their corresponding limit. The theorem is named after [[Adolf Hurwitz]].

==Statement==

Let {''f<sub>k</sub>''} be a sequence of holomorphic functions on a connected [[open set]] ''G'' that converge uniformly on [[Compact space|compact]] subsets of ''G'' to a holomorphic function ''f'' which is not constantly zero on ''G''. If ''f'' has a zero of order ''m'' at ''z''<sub>0</sub> then for every small enough ''ρ''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 and for sufficiently large ''k''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''N''' (depending on&nbsp;''ρ''),  ''f<sub>k</sub>'' has precisely ''m'' zeroes in the disk defined by |''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''z''<sub>0</sub>|&nbsp;<&nbsp;''ρ'', including [[Multiplicity (mathematics)#In complex analysis|multiplicity]].  Furthermore, these zeroes converge to ''z''<sub>0</sub> as&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;→&nbsp;∞.<ref name="Ahlfors 1966 page=176">{{harvnb|Ahlfors|1966|page=176}}, {{harvnb|Ahlfors|1978|page=178}}</ref>

==Remarks==

The theorem does not guarantee that the result will hold for arbitrary disks. Indeed, if one chooses a disk such that ''f'' has zeroes on its [[Boundary (topology)|boundary]], the theorem fails. An explicit example is to consider the [[unit disk]] '''D''' and the sequence defined by

:<math>f_n(z) = z-1+\frac 1 n, \qquad z \in \mathbb C</math>

which converges uniformly to ''f''(''z'') =&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1. The function ''f''(''z'') contains no zeroes in '''D'''; however, each ''f<sub>n</sub>'' has exactly one zero in the disk corresponding to the real value&nbsp;1&nbsp;−&nbsp;(1/''n'').

==Applications==

Hurwitz's theorem is used in the proof of the [[Riemann mapping theorem]],<ref name="Gamelin">{{Cite book | last1=Gamelin| first1=Theodore | author1-link=Theodore Gamelin | title=Complex Analysis | publisher=Springer  | isbn=978-0387950693| year=2001}}</ref> and also has the following two [[Corollary|corollaries]] as an immediate consequence:
* Let ''G'' be a connected, open set and {''f<sub>n</sub>''} a sequence of holomorphic functions which converge uniformly on compact subsets of ''G'' to a holomorphic function ''f''. If each ''f<sub>n</sub>'' is nonzero everywhere in ''G'', then ''f'' is either identically zero or also is nowhere zero.
* If {''f<sub>n</sub>''} is a sequence of [[univalent function]]s on a connected open set ''G'' that converge uniformly on compact subsets of ''G'' to a holomorphic function ''f'', then either ''f'' is univalent or constant.<ref name="Gamelin"/>

== Proof ==

Let ''f'' be an analytic function on an open subset of the complex plane with a zero of order ''m'' at ''z''<sub>0</sub>, and suppose that {''f<sub>n</sub>''} is a sequence of functions converging uniformly on compact subsets to ''f''.  Fix some ''ρ''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 such that ''f''(''z'')&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0 in 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;|''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''z''<sub>0</sub>| ≤ ρ. Choose δ such that |''f''(''z'')|&nbsp;>&nbsp;''δ'' for ''z'' on the circle |''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''z''<sub>0</sub>|&nbsp;=&nbsp;''ρ''. Since ''f<sub>k</sub>''(''z'') converges uniformly on the disc we have chosen, we can find ''N'' such that |''f<sub>k</sub>''(''z'')|&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''δ''/2 for every ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''N'' and every ''z'' on the circle, ensuring that the quotient ''f<sub>k</sub>''′(''z'')/''f<sub>k</sub>''(''z'') is well defined for all ''z'' on the circle |''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''z''<sub>0</sub>|&nbsp;=&nbsp;''ρ''.  By  Weierstrass's theorem we have <math>f_k' \to f'</math> uniformly on the disc, and hence we have another uniform convergence:

: <math>\frac{f_k'(z)}{f_k(z)} \to \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}.</math>

Denoting the number of zeros of ''f<sub>k</sub>''(''z'') in the disk by ''N<sub>k</sub>'', we may apply the [[argument principle]] to find

: <math> m = \frac 1 {2\pi i}\int_{\vert z -z_0\vert = \rho} \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)} \,dz = \lim_{k\to\infty} \frac 1 {2\pi i} \int_{\vert z -z_0\vert = \rho} \frac{f'_k(z)}{f_k(z)} \, dz = \lim_{k\to\infty} N_k</math>

In the above step, we were able to interchange the integral and the limit because of the uniform convergence of the integrand.  We have shown that ''N<sub>k</sub>''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''m'' as ''k''&nbsp;→&nbsp;∞.  Since the ''N<sub>k</sub>'' are integer valued, ''N<sub>k</sub>'' must equal ''m'' for large enough&nbsp;''k''.<ref name="Ahlfors 1966 page=176"/>
